newsitem.title: PERU: No solution in sight to Peruvian hostage drama.
newsitem.headline: No solution in sight to Peruvian hostage drama.

text.p: Marxist guerrillas holding 140 Peruvian and Japanese officials and businessmen hostage for six days showed no sign on Monday of giving up their do-or-die demands for the release of jailed comrades.

A day after freeing 225 hostages, including all the Americans, British and Germans, the well-armed Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement rebels made no new moves inside the besieged Japanese diplomatic compound.
The United States called for the immediate release of all the remaining hostages, and U.S. officials confirmed that all seven U.S. citizens that had been captives were now free.

"(President Bill Clinton) welcomes the safe release of the Americans who were held hostage in Lima and renews his call for the immediate release of all who continue to be held in the Japanese Ambassador's residence," the White House said.
"The United States will continue its close consultations with Peru, Japan, and all concerned governments on this situation," a White House statement said.
Still held inside the mansion were Peruvian President Alberto Fujimori's brother, his foreign minister, Francisco Tudela and his anti-terrorism police chief, Maximo Rivera.

The Japanese still held as bargaining chips inside the residence included Japan's ambassador, Morihisa Aoki, and top local managers of large Japanese companies who were attending a diplomatic reception when the guerrilas stormed on Tuesday.
Reflecting the grief felt in Japan, Emperor Akihito cancelled all official celebrations of his birthday on Monday.

Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto, who has taken personal control of Japan's dealings with Peruvian efforts to end the siege tracked the crisis from a special war room in the Foreign Ministry fitted out with television monitors.

Hashimoto said Tokyo's priority remained the safe release of hostages still held in the building. But he declined to comment on what steps the Japanese government will take to help bring the hostage crisis to a peaceful conclusion.
Foreign Minister Yukihiko Ikeda, who spent four days in Lima as Japan's on-the-spot adviser, returned to Tokyo on Monday evening, apparently empty-handed.
However, Ikeda's two meetings with President Fujimori did close a gap between Lima and Tokyo over how to deal with the crisis, Japanese foreign ministry officials said.

Japan endorsed Fujimori's stern call to the guerrillas to lay down their weapons and release the hostages to avoid bloodshed, shifting Tokyo's attitude from initial softness closer to Lima's hard line.

Fujimori has so far refused all the guerrillas's demands and has cut off water and electricity to the residence -- something released hostages say is endangering the health and safety of those still inside. Released hostage Victor Lucero, a physician, said at least eight cases of conjunctivitis had broken out due to the foul conditions.
The MRTA guerrillas, led by former textile factory worker turned revolutionary Nestor Cerpa, warned the Peruvian government not to try to assault the residence militarily.
British diplomat Roger Church, among those freed on Sunday, said the crisis could not be solved by force.
"I hope it will be resolved through negotiation. That is the only way out," he told a news conference. "There is not going to be a violent solution to this at all."
Church, the deputy head of mission at the British embassy in Lima, said he believed there was room for negotiation.

"The Peruvian government wants to negotiate" a way out of the crisis, Church said. He said he believed the original guerrilla demand that more than 400 comrades be freed had "been reduced somewhat" but he did not go into details.

Church and others set free said the guerrillas had not mistreated their hostages and had tried to present an image of concerned social crusaders. They said they had released most of their captives for humanitarian reasons before Christmas.
Hostages asked the rebel leader for his autograph after hours of conversation, a freed hostage was quoted by Japanese media as saying on Monday by Japan's Kyodo news agency.
Japanese officials said over 30 Japanese nationals were still captive, including top executives of the Peruvian branches Mitsubishi Corp, Toyota Motor Corp and Mitsui Mining and Smelting Co.
About 30 Japanese nationals freed by the rebels were not highly ranked or were unaffiliated with big-name businesses.
Other Japanese citizens also released on Sunday included teachers at the Japanese schools in Peru, and members of the Japan International Cooperation Agency, an aid organisation.
The guerrillas may have decided to release them after taking into account their contribution to the Peruvian people, Kyodo reported.
German diplomats said their captors had treated them well, but conditions were deplorable.
